patient.chief_complaint: Two episodes of right-sided limb weakness with left occipital headache over the past 3 weeks — sent for urgent evaluation
patient.hpi:
A 39-year-old Japanese man with a long-standing history of myofascial pain syndrome and intermittent headaches was referred to the neurology outpatient clinic for urgent evaluation after two episodes of transient right-sided limb weakness. The first episode occurred 20 days prior to this visit: he noticed weakness in his right arm and right leg while at home, along with a tense, numb feeling on the right side of his face. These symptoms developed gradually over approximately 20-25 minutes and resolved over the following 30-40 minutes. Afterwards, he experienced a left occipital headache that he treated with loxoprofen with good relief.

The second episode occurred 2 days before this visit. He was at work when he again developed right upper and lower limb weakness and a tense feeling on the left side of his mouth. He was found unresponsive by a colleague and transported by ambulance to a local emergency department. En route to hospital, he regained consciousness and complained of a left occipital headache. At the emergency department, he was alert with right limb weakness and sensory disturbance over the ulnar aspect of the right upper arm. He was admitted for observation. His symptoms gradually improved over several hours and he was discharged with an outpatient referral when no acute cause was identified.

He has a history of migraine headaches and myofascial pain, managed with lomerizine hydrochloride and as-needed NSAIDs. He has no prior stroke, no hypertension, no diabetes, and no cardiac disease. He is a non-smoker. He reports no family history of hemiplegic migraine. He is now headache-free and fully neurologically intact at this consultation.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Sporadic hemiplegic migraine (ICHD-3 1.2.3) — two qualifying episodes with gradual motor and sensory aura followed by headache; all secondary causes excluded

differential.key_features: Motor aura always requires TIA exclusion; normal MRI/MRA excludes acute infarction and large-vessel disease
No family history; sporadic form more likely
No neck pain or trauma; MRA shows no dissection
Aura duration too long for seizure propagation

optimal_actions.expected_finding: ICHD-3 criteria for migraine with aura confirmed; no SNOOP red flag present that mandates further workup

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions and contraindications for acute (triptan/ergotamine/CGRP antagonist) and prophylactic (beta-blocker, topiramate, valproate, amitriptyline) migraine medications appropriate to this patient
optimal_actions.expected_finding: TRIPTANS AND ERGOTAMINES CONTRAINDICATED in hemiplegic migraine — use NSAIDs, antiemetics, or gepants/lasmiditan

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI with MRA to exclude structural / vascular cause

Take a structured headache and aura history against ICHD-3 1.2: number of attacks, aura modality and full reversibility, gradual spread over at least five minutes, duration of each symptom between five and sixty minutes, unilaterality, temporal relation to the headache, and a documented red-flag review. This is the diagnostic test for this condition
optimal_actions.expected_finding: ICHD-3 1.2 criteria documented item by item against the reference set for this subtype, with the red-flag review recorded

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic / bubble echocardiogram (PFO screening) is NOT indicated in migraine with aura; PFO-migraine association is controversial and PFO closure does not reduce migraine [Charles_2017]

critical_actions: Brain MRI/MRA required at first hemiplegic migraine presentation
Use NSAIDs, antiemetics, gepants/lasmiditan for acute therapy
Consider preventive therapy if recurrent episodes (topiramate, verapamil) [Holland_2012]
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe triptans or ergotamines in hemiplegic migraine
Do not co-administer ergotamines with triptans
key_reasoning_points: Two qualifying episodes meet ICHD-3 criteria when motor aura is fully reversible
TIA exclusion via MRI/MRA is mandatory at first presentation of motor aura
Triptans are contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: ICHD-3: the diagnosis is made on the structured history. Imaging is for the red flags that history screens for, not for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Right-sided limb weakness in a 39-year-old man
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gradual motor + sensory aura over minutes with subsequent migrainous headache is hemiplegic migraine after TIA is excluded by normal MRI/MRA

red_herrings.data_point: Transient loss of consciousness at second episode — suggesting seizure or cardiac arrhythmia
red_herrings.intended_effect: Brief loss of consciousness is not a classic hemiplegic migraine feature — raises concern for seizure (Todd's paralysis) or cardiogenic syncope
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Loss of consciousness can occur in severe hemiplegic migraine (impaired consciousness is a recognised aura feature); normal EEG excludes seizure; normal Holter excludes arrhythmia; gradual onset remains the key differentiating feature

clinical_assessment.impression: Structured headache and aura history taken against ICHD-3 1.2. 4 of the four criterion-C characteristics are documented — this presentation is hemiplegic migraine (ICHD-3 1.2.3), which requires motor weakness in addition to the 1.2 criteria; the weakness is documented, and the diagnosis is met on the history. The distinction from a transient ischaemic attack is made here and not by imaging: aura spreads gradually over minutes and is positive before it is negative, whereas ischaemia is abrupt and negative from the outset. Imaging is for the red flags this history screens for, not for the diagnosis.

output.summary: DRUG REVIEW — TRIPTANS IN HEMIPLEGIC MIGRAINE FINDINGS: Triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists) exert vasoconstrictive effects on cerebral and meningeal vasculature. In the context of hemiplegic migraine — where motor aura is associated with cortical spreading depression and haemodynamic changes — most international guidelines caution against triptan use during motor aura episodes due to theoretical vasoconstrictive risk, although the evidence base is limited. CATEGORY: Triptans are cautioned (not universally absolutely contraindicated) in hemiplegic migraine; individual guideline recommendations vary. Clinical correlation recommended. Triptans are cautioned in hemiplegic migraine due to theoretical vasoconstrictive risk during motor aura; category-level caution applies;
